cultivar: Assam-type and hybrid seedling bushes plus UPASI clones
processing: Mostly CTC for the Indian market; a few estates and small producers make fully oxidised orthodox leaf grades and speciality teas.
harvest_season: Year-round; the cooler, drier months from December to March give the brightest teas.
appearance_dry: Black granules for CTC, or twisted dark leaf for orthodox lots.
taste_profile: Bright and brisk with a mild malty sweetness and a light fruity edge; less fragrant than Nilgiri but with more body.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, 3–4 minutes, milk optional; orthodox lots give a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold year-round through the Kochi auction and in Kerala as packet tea (Kanan Devan Hills Plantations is the big name), with orthodox and 'speciality' lots from estates such as Kolukkumalai appearing in small quantities with a season and year. No vintage: buy fresh and use within a year.
description:
Munnar black tea comes from the High Range of Kerala in south-west India, where tea has been grown since around 1880 on the rolling hills around the town of Munnar at roughly 1,500 to 2,500 metres. It is one of the biggest tea districts of the Western Ghats and the source of most of Kerala's packet tea.

The gardens, once the Kannan Devan Hills Produce Company and now mostly the employee-owned Kanan Devan Hills Plantations, make the great bulk of their leaf as CTC for the Indian market. A few estates and small producers also make orthodox leaf grades and speciality teas, and the Kolukkumalai estate, just over the state line in Tamil Nadu at around 2,400 metres, sells its orthodox tea as grown on the world's highest tea plantation.

The cup is bright reddish-amber, brisk and clean with a mild malty sweetness and a light fruity edge; it has more body than a Nilgiri but less fragrance. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes, with milk if you like; the orthodox lots give a second steep.

It is sold year-round through the Kochi auction and in Kerala as packet tea, with orthodox and 'speciality' lots from named estates appearing in small quantities with the season and year. The cooler, drier months from December to March give the brightest teas. There is no vintage: buy fresh and use within a year.

It is also one of the most visited tea landscapes in India, and the tea museum in Munnar is a good place to see old CTC and orthodox machinery at work.
sources_note: Native name in Malayalam. No dedicated Wikipedia article for Munnar tea; the town article is used as the umbrella. 'World's highest tea plantation' is Kolukkumalai's own marketing claim.
